primary_claim: A three-stage classifier (regex screen, small prompted LLM, large prompted LLM) for filtering 'narrow scheming data' from AI training corpora achieves acceptable precision on a hand-audited, web-scraped sensitive-content sample (13 of 15 flagged documents judged correctly filtered), while screening out the large majority of a random corpus sample as not needing filtering.

effect.metric: manual audit precision of classifier-flagged documents
effect.value: 13/15 audited flagged documents judged correctly filtered (2 false positives)

contradicts_or_qualifies: CBRN/bio-misuse pretraining data filtering approaches, which the author argues face different dynamics than narrow scheming data filtering
stated_future_work: Discuss a more aggressive filtering proposal (removing discussion of AI misalignment/deceptive alignment from training data) in a future post.
Empirically study how strongly filtering reduces the salience of widely-spread concepts such as 'we do CoT monitoring'.
limitations_stated: 2 of 15 audited filtered documents were false positives -- sensitive topics discussed at an extremely high level that ideally would not have been filtered.
Filtering is imperfect; AI systems may still obtain filtered information via web search, users, or reasoning.
It's unclear how strongly filtering reduces the salience of widely-spread concepts rather than removing specific pieces of information.
quote: I ran my entire classifier system on this dataset, and audited 15 of the filtered documents. Of these, I was happy with 13 of the 15 documents; the 2 "false positives" were documents that discuss sensitive topics at an extremely high level.
